# Presentation patterns {#sec-patterns}

The layers of @sec-layers say *where* code lives. A presentation pattern says how the view
and the code behind it talk. Qt Quick works best with two of them: MVVM for most screens,
Flux for documents with a history.

## From MVC to MVVM {#sec-mvc-mvvm}

Three patterns share the same goal (keeping logic out of the view) but differ in who updates
the view:

| Pattern | How the view gets updated | Where you meet it in Qt |
|---|---|---|
| **MVC** | the view reads the model; a controller handles input | Qt's model/view classes: an item model, a view, a delegate |
| **MVP** | a presenter pushes every value into a passive view | many Qt Widgets applications |
| **MVVM** | the view *binds* to a view model; nothing pushes | Qt Quick |

MVVM fits Qt Quick because bindings do the updating. The view model only has to change its
properties and emit their signals.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 6.5
flowchart LR
    V["View<br/>(QML)"] -- "calls commands" --> VM["ViewModel<br/>(C++)"]
    VM -. "properties and signals,<br/>picked up by bindings" .-> V
    VM -- "reads and writes" --> M["Model<br/>(core, storage)"]
```

## MVVM {#sec-mvvm}

A view model offers **state** as properties and **commands** as invokable methods. The view
binds to the state and calls the commands. It decides nothing.

```{.cpp filename="SketchbookViewModel.hpp"}
class SketchbookViewModel : public QObject
{
    Q_OBJECT
    QML_ELEMENT
    QML_UNCREATABLE("Created in main()")
    Q_PROPERTY(SketchListModel *model READ model CONSTANT FINAL)            // <1>
    Q_PROPERTY(QString openName READ openName NOTIFY openNameChanged FINAL)

public:
    Q_INVOKABLE void create();                                               // <2>
    Q_INVOKABLE void rename(int row, const QString &name);
    Q_INVOKABLE void remove(int row);
    // ...
};
```
1. State: the list of sketches and the name of the open one.
2. Commands: what the user can do. Validation and storage happen behind them.

```{.qml filename="SketchbookPage.qml"}
Button {
    text: qsTr("New sketch")
    onClicked: root.viewModel.create()
}
```

The view model contains no QML and no visual types, so a plain Qt Test can drive it: call
`create()`, then check the model's row count (@sec-test-layers).

::: {.more}
**Template:** `src/sketchbook/`
:::

## Flux {#sec-flux}

Flux sends every change along one path. The view dispatches an **action**; a pure function,
the **reducer**, computes the next state from the current state and the action; the
**store** keeps the result and notifies the views.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    V["View"] -- "action" --> S["Store"]
    S -- "state + action" --> R["reduce()"]
    R -- "new state" --> S
    S -. "changed" .-> V
```

In C++, actions are a `std::variant` and the reducer visits it:

```{.cpp filename="Sketch.hpp"}
using StrokePtr = std::shared_ptr<const Stroke>;   // <1>
using Sketch = std::vector<StrokePtr>;

struct AddStroke { StrokePtr stroke; };
struct Clear {};
using Action = std::variant<AddStroke, Clear>;

template <typename... Fs>
struct Overloaded : Fs... { using Fs::operator()...; };

Sketch reduce(Sketch sketch, const Action &action)    // <2>
{
    std::visit(Overloaded{
        [&](const AddStroke &add) { sketch.push_back(add.stroke); },
        [&](Clear) { sketch.clear(); },
    }, action);
    return sketch;
}
```
1. A stroke never changes once drawn, so every state shares it instead of copying it.
2. Pure: the same sketch and action always give the same result. A new action type that
   `reduce()` forgets to handle fails to compile.

Because each state is a value, keeping old states gives undo and redo almost for free:

```{.cpp filename="CanvasStore.cpp"}
void CanvasStore::dispatch(const Action &action)
{
    auto next = reduce(m_history[m_current], action);
    m_history.resize(m_current + 1);            // <1>
    m_history.push_back(std::move(next));
    m_current = m_history.size() - 1;
    Q_EMIT changed();
}

void CanvasStore::undo()
{
    if (m_current > 0) {
        --m_current;                            // <2>
        Q_EMIT changed();
    }
}
```
1. A new edit drops the states that were undone.
2. Undo moves a cursor back. No action needs an inverse.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `src/canvas/Sketch.hpp`, `src/canvas/CanvasStore.cpp`
:::

## Choosing a pattern {#sec-choosing}

| Your screen | Pattern |
|---|---|
| Lists, forms, settings: state that maps onto controls | MVVM |
| Editors and documents whose history matters: undo, autosave, replay | Flux |
| Pure presentation: a dialog that only shows values | plain QML with required properties |

One app can mix them, one pattern per feature. The template does exactly that: the
sketchbook is MVVM, the canvas is Flux.

For very large documents, copying even a vector of pointers per edit becomes expensive.
At that point, look into persistent data structures, which share unchanged parts
automatically.
